ORAL ANSWERS TO 
QUESTIONS Collapse of colliery 
*221. SHRI LALIT SURI: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether the roof of an abandon ed CCL, Colliery near Hazaribag 
collapsed on 28 th/29th September, 2005 leading to  the death of a number of 
persons engaged in illegal mining there; 
(b) if so, the number of the persons who lost their lives in the mishap; 
(c) whether the matter has been investigated as to the role of unauthorized 
contractors/officials of the CCL, and others in the illegal mining which led to 
the mishap; and 
(d) if so, the findings thereof and the action taken thereon? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN TH E MINISTRY OF COAL (DR. 
DASARI NARAYAN RAO): (a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table of 
the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) Yes Sir, a portion of mine roof collapsed at Section-I quarry of 
Rajrappa Project of Central Coalfiel ds Ltd. near Hazaribagh, Jharkhand 
while illegal mining was being done on 29.9.2005. The Officer Incharge of 
Rajrappa Police Station in his report dated 29.9.2005 has mentioned that two 
bodies were recovered from the accident site. 
(c) and (d) The police has registered a case vide Rajrappa Police outpost 
(Police Station, Ramgarh), case No. 399/05 dated 29.9.05 under sections 
286,287,338,379,304(A) of the Indian Penal Code and Section 30(ii) of the 
Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973 and the matter is under enquiry by 
the police.

RAJYA SABHA [8 December, 2005] 
SHRI LALIT SURI: Sir, this is not  the first case in which workers 
engaged by contractors in illegal mining have been killed. Obviously, in such 
activities, contractors and employees of local companies and the local 
administration are involved and act jo intly. My question to the hon. Prime 
Minister is this. What specific action has been taken against those found to 
be involved in such activities and what compensation is being given for the 
people who have been killed? 
DR. DASARI NARAYAN RAO: This  is about accidents in illegal 
mining. This has nothing to do with the management of the Coal India Ltd. 
There are mines which have been abandoned and there are mines which have 
been closed. There, some illegal mining is taking place. We have observed 
that illegal mining is linked with socio-economic problems, as also the law 
and order problem. Sir, one can see, and I have also personally witnessed, at 
these places, hundreds of people carrying gunny bags full of coal on their 
cycles. No contractor is hired by the company. There are private people 
involved there. Whatever accidents ta ke place, they do not come on the 
record of the police. That is how th ings are happening there. This is 
absolutely illegal mining and it is not in the hands of the contractors. 
SHRI LALIT SURI: Sir, my second s upplementary is this. India has one 
of the largest reserves of coal in the world. The hon. Prime Minister is very 
keen on this, and there is a Bill pending in the Rajya Sabha for privitisation 
and for using the most modern techniqu es to mine the coal. I would like to 
ask the hon. Prime Minister how he will proceed further to get the Bill 
through, as soon as possible, so that th e coal which is already there can be 
mined in a scientific manner and the cost of generation of power which is 
very high can be reduced. 
DR. DASARI NARAYAN RAO: Sir, this  does not pertain to the main 
question. But still, for the convenience of the hon. Member, I would like to 
reply to it. The hon. Member is aware that the Coalmine (Amendment) Bill, 
2000 is pending in this House. There have been a lot of protests from the 
trade unions and our friends from the Left. Unless there is unanimity on the 
issue, I don't think the Bill can be passed. That is number one. The second 
one is with regard to meeting the demand. Sir, it does not mean that we are 
not in a position to meet the demand. We have increased the production. But, 
there is also a rapid demand to that extent. Our growth rate, as per the vision 
of the hon. Prime Minister, should reach 10 per cent. Looking at the vision of 
hon. Prime Minister, a rapid increase in production is very much needed. 
And, to meet the demand, we have allocated nearly

media, NGOs, Training to Drivers, etc. 
• Widening and improvements of National Highways with divided 
carriageways. 
• Improvement of junctions/intersections. 
• Rectification of deficient road geometry of National Highways. 
• Provision of bypasses and flyovers/grade separators. 
• Improvement in road markings/signs.

Shortage of coal for small/medium scale coal consuming 
industries 
231. SHRI DEVDAS APTE: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether there is acute shortage of coal for small/medium scale coal 
consuming industries in the country and the power sector, consuming almost 
all the coal produced domestically, is enjoying priority of allocation and 
preference of price; 
(b) whether small and medium scale coal consuming industries, especially 
those which mushroomed in coal produ cing States in the past, are meeting 
their demand by buying coal from 'market'  at more than three times the price 
paid by power sector; and 
(c) the steps proposed to get sufficient coal to such industries to meet, the 
demand? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COAL (DR. 
DASARI NARAYAN RAO): (a) Around 80% of coal produced by Coal 
India Limited is consumed by power sector and in view of criticality of 
power sector in the country, highest priority is given to the power sector in 
supply of coal. This has resulted in shortage of coal availability to small and 
medium industries. Because of high pri ces of coal in international markets 
expected import of coal has also not  materialized further increasing the 
demand for coal from power sector. 
(b) In order to equitably distribute available coal, a transparent method of 
sale of coal through e-auction has been started by Coal India Limited. The 
average price of e-auction coal is about 56% higher than the notified price 
and not three times the price paid by power sector. Apart from this 5 million 
tonnes of coal is being released fo r small scale industries through State 
Government notified undertakings and NCCF at concessional price (20% 
above notified price). 
(c) Following steps have been taken to increase availability of coal: 
(i)   CIL has been requested to increase its production. 
(ii) Power sector has been requested to import 13.45 million tonnes of 
coal so that additional indigenous  coal becomes available to small 
and medium industries.

sector companies in order to enhance coal production. 
(iv) 10 million tonnes of coal is offered under E-auction sale during the 
year 2005-06 to increase availability of coal to the non-linked 
consumers.

COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY (DR.

villages with population more than 2000 and not having a PCO. 
These RCPs wil be provided in a time bound manner by September 
2007.15,946 RCPs have been provided till 30.9.2005.

demand in 1,685 commercially unviable Short Distance Charging 
Areas (SDCAs) by first quarter of the year 2006.

Losses to KVI 
†1648. SHRIMATI KUM KUM RAI: Will the Minister of AGRO AND 
RURAL INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Khadi and Village Industry are running at a loss; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(c) the measures taken to prevent this loss? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRO AND  RURAL INDUSTRIES (SHRI 
MAHAVIR PRASAD): (a) to (c) The info rmation in respect of profit/ loss 
making khadi and village industry (KVI) units is not maintained centrally. 
However, some KVI units/ institutions do suffer losses. The reasons for such 
losses include use of obsolete technology, inconsistent quality of products, 
lack of designs in keeping with market demand, lack of entrepreneurial and 
managerial skills, etc. 
In order to help the KVI units/ institutions improve their viability on a 
sustainalble basis, incentives like product quality testing at subsidized rates, 
financial assistance for participation in exhibitions at the national and sub-
national levels, assistance for creation of packaging and design facilities, 
assistance for marketing, brand building, publicity etc. , are provided by the 
Government through Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC).

RURAL INDUSTRIES be pleased to state:

village industries by bank-loans under REGP schemes, because they cannot

THE MINISTER OF AGRO AND RURAL INDUSTRIES (SHRI 
MAHAVIR PRASAD): (a) As per Reserve Bank of India's (RBI) 
instructions to the banks, collateral security is not required to be furnished by 
eligible entrepreneurs for securing loan of upto Rs. 5 lakh for setting up 
small scale, including village industry (VI), units under the Rural 
Employment Generation Programme (REGP). The Credit Guarantee Trust 
for Small Industries (CGTSI) has also advised its member lending 
institutions to cover loans of upto Rs. 25 lakh extended to VI units under 
REGP under CGTSI's credit guarantee so that small entrepreneurs, including

(b) Khadi units are not eligible for assistance under the REGP. 
(c) The REGP, a credit-linked subsidy programme implemented through 
the Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC), assists eligible 
entrepreneurs in setting up labour-intensive industries in the rural areas and 
small towns with populations up to 20,000. Under this programme, 
entrepreneurs can establish village industries by availing of margin money 
assistance (Government grants) from  the KVIC and loans from any public 
sector scheduled commercial bank, for projects with a maximum cost of Rs. 
25 lakh. Under the REGP, 2,09,705 projects have been financed since its 
commencement, generating 28. 06 lakh additional employment upto 31 
March, 2005 and a sum of Rs 1372 crore has been released as margin money 
assistance to entrepreneurs.

1653. SHR B.K. HARIPRASAD: Will the PRIME MINISTER be

underground coal gasification process which is already in operation at 
Australia's Chichilla Project;

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COAL (DR. 
DASARI NARAYAN RAO): (a) A total of about 248 billion tonnes of coal 
resources have been estimatedjay Geological Survey of India (as on 1.1.05). 
Out of these about 93 billion tonnes are in 'Proved' category for which project

billion tonnes (1,55,000 million tonnes are in 'Indicated' and 'Inferred' 
categories). The reserves in 'Indicated and' 'Inferred' categories may be

resources however, depends on the economics and the state of technology.

underground coal gasification projects. The joint venture of CIL and ONGC

1655. SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased

DASARI NARAYAN RAO): (a) and (b) Mining of coal in India is broadly 
governed by the Mines Act 1952, the Mines & Minerals (Development & 
Regulation) Act 1957, the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act 1973, the

statutes in mines in the country. Prompt action is taken by the coal

An incident of sudden slide of O.B. occurred on 25th August, 2001 when 
the P&H 1900 Shovel No. 8 was working near 8 hillock which had a crack 
and could not be noticed during regular mine inspection. This shovel was 
partially damaged, which was taken out for repair on the 3rd day of the 
incident. The present cost of this model shovel is approximately Rs. 16 
crores. This shovel is not new and this shovel was commissioned on 
6/8/1999. 
The incident was thoroughly enquir ed and examined by a committee 
consisting of senior officers. While attributing the presence of hidden slip, 
which could not be noticed during regular mine inspection, as the root cause 
responsible for the accident, the commi ttee found the shif t incharge and 
Section Manager of the coal company responsible for failing of their duties 
and not taking necessary precautions. They were issued warning letters. 
The shovel was recommissioned on 1 st  January, 2003 after necessary 
repairs. The total cost of repairs including parts was Rs. 2.89 crores. 
(c) As reported by Coal India Limited it is not a fact that shovel machine 
worth Rs. 8 crores belonging to Khadia Project was damaged completely in 
an accident last year. However, on 23rd October, 2004, at about 8.30 PM, the 
BE-195 10 Cubic Metre Shovel having CIL No. EXC-1696, named Vikas 
was partially damaged during the idle hours, due to sudden slide of Dragline 
dump. The machine was kept at safe distance. In spite of all precautions 
taken as stipulated by Department of Mines and other agencies

adjusted with its annual maintena nce period. Hence, there was not

approximately (2.84% of the cost of the shovel), to bring the shovel 
in state of full fledged operation. 
(iii) Though the shovel was out of op eration for three and half months, 
still the coal production (in which the shovel was deployed) for the 
financial year 2004-05 was Rs. 39.33 lakhs tonnes against the 
targeted production of 38 lakhs tonnes, which is highest ever since 
inception of mine. 
(e) (i)   In case of Jayant Project as already mentioned in reply to parts

have been issued to Shift Incharge and Section Manager. 
(ii) In case of Khadia Project sin ce the incident took place much after

Statement 
Copy of the press note issued by Ministry of Commerce and Industry 
Government of India 
Ministry of Commerce & Industry 
Department of Industrial Policy & Promotion 
Secretariat for Industrial Assistance 
PRESS NOTE NO. 5 (2005 SERIES) 
Subject:   Enhancement of the Foreign Direct Investment ceiling from 49th 
per cent to 74 per cent in the Telecom sector. 
1. In pursuance of the Government's commitment to liberalise the FDI 
regime, it has been decided to enhance the Foreing Direct Investment ceiling 
from 49 per cent to 74 per cent in certa in telecom services [such as Basic, 
Cellular, Unified Access Services, National/International long Distance, V-
Sat, Public Mobile Radio Trunked Services (PMRTS), Global Mobile 
Personal Communications Services (GMPCS) and other value added 
services], subject to the following conditions:— 
A. The total composite foreign holding including hut not limited to 
investments by Foreign Institutional Investors (Flls), Non-Resident 
Indians (NRIs), Foreign Currenc y Convertible Bonds (FCCBs), 
American Depository Receipts (ADRs), Global Depository Receipts 
(GDRs), convertible preference shares, proportionate foreign 
86 

[8 December, 2005] RAJYASABHA 
investment in Indian promoters/investment companies including 
their holding companies, etc., here inafter referred as FDI, will not 
exceed 74 per cent. Thus, 74 per cent foreing investment can be 
made directly or indirectly in the operating company or through a 
holding company. Hence, the rema ining 26 per cent will be owned 
by resident Indian citizens or an Indian Company (i.e. Foreign 
Direct Investment does not exceed  49 per cent and the management 
is with the Indian owners). It is clarified that proportionate foreign 
component of such as Indian Company will also be counted towards 
the ceiling of 74%. However, foreign component in the total 
holding of Indian public sector banks and Indian public sector 
financial institutions will be treated as 'Indian' holding. The licensee 
will be required to disclose the status of such foreign holding and 
certify that the foreign investment is within the ceiling of 74% on a 
half yearly basis. 
B. The majority Directors on th e Board including Chairman, Managing 
Director and Chief Executive Officer (CEO) shall be resident Indian 
citizens, enforced through licen ce agreement. The appointment 
to these positions from among resi dent Indian citizens shall be 
made in consultation with serious Indian investors. Serious investor 
has been defined below inpara G(ii). 
C. The share Holder Agreements (S HA) shall specifically incorporate 
the condition that majority directors on the Board including 
Chairman, Managing Director and CEO shall be resident Indian 
citizens and shall also envisage the conditions of adherence to 
Licence Agreement. 
D. FDI upto 49 per cent will continue to be on automatic route. Foreign 
Investment Promotion Board (FIPB) approval shall be required for 
FDI in the licensee company/In dian promoters/investment 
companies including their holding companies if it has a bearing 
on the overall ceiling of 74 per cent. While approving the 
investment 
proposals, FIPB shall take note that investment is not coming 
from unfriendly countries. 
E. The investment approval by FIPB shall envisage the conditionality 
that Company would adhere to licence Agreement. 
F. FDI shall be subject to laws of India and not the laws of the foreign 
country/countries. 
87 

RAJYA SABHA [8 December, 2005] 
(G) Department of Telecommunications (DoT) will enforce the above 
and the conditions mentioned below through appropriate 
amendment in licence:- 
(i) There shall be a non-obstante  clause in the licence which 
confers powers upon the licensor to cancel the licence under 
certain defined circumstances. 
(ii) In order to ensure that at least one serious resident Indian 
promoter subscribes reasonable amount of the resident Indian 
shareholding, such resident Indian promoter shall hold at least 
10 per cent equity of the licensee company. 
(iii) The Company shall acknowledge compliance with the licence 
agreement as a part of Memorandum of Association of the 
Company. Any violation of the licence agreement shall 
automatically lead to the company being unable to carry on its 
business in this regard. The duty to comply with the licence 
agreement shall also be made a part of Articles of Association.

shall be resident Indian Citizens. The Licensor/DoT shall also 
be empowered to notify key positions to be held by resident 
Indian citizens. 
(v) The Company shall not transfer the following to any person/ 
place outside India.- 
(a) any accounting information relating to subscriber (except 
for raming/billing) (Note: it does not restrict a statutorily 
required disclosure of financial nature); 
(b) user information (except pertaining to foreign subscribers 
using Indian Operator's network while roaming) and 
(c) details of their infrastructur e/network diagram except to 
telecom equipment suppliers/manufactures who undertake 
the installation, commissioning etc.  of the infrastructure of

†1760.SHRI RAJ MOHINDER SINGH MAJITHA: 
SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD: 
Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that per capita monthly expenditure of the families 
of farmers of rural areas in the country was Rs. 503/- in 2003; 
(b) if not, the facts in this regard; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that this amount is Rs. 75/- more than the 
criteria of poverty Iine; 
(d) if not, the criteria fixed for poverty line; and 
(e) the average number of the families living below the poverty line in the 
country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING 
(SHRI M.V. RAJASEKHARAN): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. According to the 
results of the Situation Assessment Survey of Farmers conducted by NSSO 
(59th round, Jan-Dec, 2003)-compiled in the Report No. 495- the average 
monthly per capita total consumption expenditure of a farmer household at 
the national level was Rs. 502.83. 
(c) No, Sir. The Planning Commission estimates poverty at national 
and State level from the large samp le survey on household consumer 
expenditure conducted by the National Sample Survey Organisation 
(NSSO) at an interval of  approximately five years. The rural poverty line 
at the national level estimated from the latest available data of such Survey 
(NSS 55th round, 1999-2000) is Rs. 327.56 
The average monthly total consumption expenditure of farmers of Rs. 
502.83 deflated to 1999-2000 prices works out to Rs. 487.97. Therefore, the 
difference between the two is Rs. 160.41 at 1999-2000 price. 
(d) Planning Commission uses per capita consumption expenditure as 
the criteria to determine the poverty line. 
The main factors, which are taken into consideration in arriving at the 
figure of poverty line, are based on the methodology recommended by the 
Expert Group on 'Estimation of Proportion and Number of Poor' (Lakdawala 
Committee). The Expert Group, which was constituted in September, 1989 
submitted its Report to the Planning Commission in July, 1993. A full 
Planning Commission meeting chaired by the Prime Minister in March, 1997 
accepted the recommendations of the Expert 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
162 

[8 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Group with minor modifications. Since then the estimates of poverty at 
national and State level are being made using the Expert Group methodology. 
The per capita consumption norm has been fixed at Rs. 49.09 per month in 
rural areas at 1973-74 prices at national level corresponding to a basket of 
goods and services anchored on a norm of per capita daily calorie 
requirement of 2400 kcal in rural areas. The prescribed per capita 
consumption expenditure limit in rural areas is then updated using State-
specific cost of living indices for Ag ricultural Labourers (CPIAL) for rural 
areas. The national poverty line at 1999-2000 prices is Rs. 327.56 per capita 
per month in rural areas. 
(e) The percentage of persons living below the poverty line in the country 
was 26.10 during 1999-2000, according to the 55th round of NSS Household 
Consumer Expenditure Survey. The co rresponding figures are 27.09 and 
23.62 for rural and urban areas respectively. The Planning Commission does 
not estimate the number of families living below poverty line.

(c) As per Section 358 of Merchant Shipping Act, 1958, a shipping 
casualty shall be deemed to occur when: 
(i) on or near the coasts of Indian, any ship is lost, abandoned, stranded 
or materially damaged; 
(ii) on or near the coasts of Indi an, any ship causes loss or material 
damage to any other ship; 
(iii) any loss of life ensues by reason of any casualty happening to or on 
board any ship on or near the coasts of India; 
(iv) in any place, any such loss, abandonment, stranding, material 
damage or casualty as above mentioned occurs to or on board any 
Indian ship, and any competept witness thereof is found in India; 
(v) any Indian ship is lost or is supposed to have been lost and any 
evidence is obtainable in India as to the circumstances under which 
she proceeded to sea or was heard of; 
In all such cases, the appointed officer makes the preliminary inquiry into 
the casaulty. However, no investigati on is conducted under the Merchant 
Shipping Act, 1958 in casualities falling out side the purview of section 358

SHRI MANI SHANKAR AIYAR: Mr Chairman, Sir, I am, indeed, most 
grateful to all the hon. Members repres enting, virtually, all the parties in the 
House as well as many of the differe nt regions of the country for having 
participated in this discussion. It has been enlightening for me, and I trust that 
after I have given clarifications sough t, we will be able to concentrate our 
minds constructively on what more, perhaps, needs to be done, I shall start 
appropriately with comrade Dipankar Mukherjee who initiated the discussion, 
and, his primary question, his initial questi on to me was: "How is it that the 
shot down was taken by a private refine r, precisely, at the time when the 
festival season was on? Sir, all I can say is that we were notified, as long ago 
as last year, that because that hadn't ta ken a shutdown, particularly, in their 
FCC unit, since the commissioning of the plant, they would have to do so, 
and they indicated a period to us which was outside of the festive season. 
Since the notification had come to us well in time, arrangements were made 
for effecting imports to be able to make up for the gap that was anticipated at 
that time. But, there

Sir, I have been asked as to why the PSUs should suffer a loss on each 
cylinder. I have been asked: Is it true that because the PSUs are suffering a 
loss on every cylinder, they are reluctant to effect supplies? 
Now, the fact of the matter is that no commercial company is going to be 
enthusiastic about adding to its losses. But what we have to ask oruselves is: 
Can we solve this problem without, at anyrate, increasing the magnitude of 
the losses? After all, this year, though we have so strictly controlled the prices

extremely important point as to whether

dimension of the problem as well As far as our own companies are

As regards the distinction between the BPL and the APL, when it comes to 
questions of Kerosene, I need to draw upon this extremely important and the 
first-ever scientific study done of the demand for kerosene in our country. It 
was done by the National Council of Applied Economic Research and it was 
given to us a little over a month ago. I am not going to waste the time of the 
House with figures. But some of the findi ngs are very, very interesting. One is 
that BPL families, especially in rural areas, have a much greater awareness of 
their entitlements for kerosene than APL families. This is because the BPL 
families need kerosene much more that the APL families do. The second very 
important finding that comes out is that, probably, diversion of various kinds is 
greater in the urban areas th at it is in the rural areas  and greater still in the 
metropolitan areas than it is in the mofussil areas I think we need to draw 
policy decisions out of this. So, we have brought all these conclusions to the 
attention of State Govern ments. We are interacting with them. And we hope 
that we can produce a policy eventually wh ich will actually tackle the sources 
from which this diversion, one, to adulteration and, two, to the black market for 
resale takes place so as the be able more to focus the availability of PDS 
kerosene to those who are really in need of it. In this connection, I would like 
to respond to Shri Jairam Ramesh's point about the demand for kerosene 
having remained almost steady over the last ten years. He is surprised; I am 
not; the reason being that, as rural el ectrification increases, while rural 
electrification does not meet the entire  demand for lighting our rural areas or 
even of the rural poor, it does decreas e progressively the need for kerosene. 
In deed, we find that there are a lot of APL families who also keep kerosene 
because although electricity is made available, its reliability factor is somewhat 
limited. So, people wish to have a back-up facility. Nobody who can actually 
use the electricity would really prefer to use the kerosene. But, if the electricity 
facility is there, but electricity itself is not actually delivered, then, they do need 
to have kerosene as a back-up facility. Similarly, there has been a spread, a 
very weak spread, I agree with Shri Jairam Ramesh, of LPG to rural areas. 
But, to the extent to which it has taken place, it is replacing the need for 
kerosene. So, the increase in population is leading to an increase in demand 
for kerosene. But, at the same time, th e replacement of kerosene by rural 
electrification and LPG is diminishing the extent to which a given family is in 
need of kerosene, and the trade-off between
